name: Mapuche tayil genealogical chant
lineage: Mapuche (Araucanian) tayil women's genealogical-ritual chant tradition of the Mapuche communities of southern Argentina (Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut provinces) and adjacent southern-central Chile (Araucanía Region). Tayil is a sung-evocation of a kin-group's tayil-spirit (each Mapuche kin-group / küpan has its own tayil-spirit-melody, inherited matrilineally), with the singer's voice bringing-present the spiritual essence of the ancestor-line during the ngillatún collective-ceremony (the central Mapuche public ritual cycle, held over multiple days in a sacred clearing). Performance involves a single woman singer-evocator (tayilfe) in melismatic-narrow-range melodic style with characteristic descending-contour cadential conventions and Mapuche pentatonic-leaning modal vocabulary, accompanied by kultrún (the one-headed shamanic frame-drum with cosmological-diagram-painted goat-skin or horse-skin head, struck with a curved beater) and sometimes trutruka long-trumpet or pifüllka end-blown whistles. The tayil tradition is distinct from but adjacent to the machi shamanic ülkantun (the curing-songs of the machi shaman, a separate role and repertoire). Carol E. Robertson-DeCarbo's 1976 Indiana doctoral dissertation (Tayil: Musical Communication and Social Organization Among the Mapuche of Argentina), her 1979 Ethnomusicology article Pulling the Ancestors (23/3), and María Ester Grebe Vicuña's 1973 Revista Musical Chilena article on the kultrún constitute the foundational scholarship. Distinguished from neighboring Tehuelche and Huilliche vocal traditions by Mapuche-Mapudungun language and tayil-spirit-evocation functional framework; distinguished from broader South American indigenous ritual-music by the specific küpan-spirit-inheritance kin-group structure.
